h1: How an airbag works: what happens in 40 milliseconds
lead: The airbag in the steering wheel is not a “firecracker” but a chain of a sensor, a control unit, an igniter, an inflator and fabric that fires faster than you can blink. We go through what the module is made of, what happens in the first 40 milliseconds and which parts are replaced after deployment — this matters if a lot listing says the airbags deployed.

card.title: How an airbag works: what happens in 40 milliseconds
card.text: What the steering wheel module is made of, what happens in the first 40 milliseconds after impact, which parts are replaced after deployment and what not to do during repair.

og.s: What happens in 40 milliseconds and what to replace after deployment

summary: **The SRS control unit decides, not the airbag:** it calculates the change in speed from the crash sensor signal and sends current to the igniter — usually within the first 10–30 milliseconds after impact.
**The inflator makes the gas:** solid propellant tablets burn in a few tens of milliseconds; by 30–50 ms the airbag is inflated, and by 100–150 ms it is already deflating through the vent holes.
**The airbag works together with the seat belt:** the belt carries the main load and limits the force, while the airbag spreads the rest over the area of the chest and head.
**After deployment, more than the airbags are replaced:** the SRS control unit, seat belt pretensioners, often the dashboard and the steering wheel; the clock spring and sensors are checked.
**The most dangerous thing is “dummies”:** emulators instead of airbags and counterfeit modules make the car look fine but do not protect.

blocks.x: Below is the typical sequence in a frontal crash when the driver is belted. Exact values depend on the make, the control unit algorithm and the specific module, so we give orders of magnitude, not data-sheet figures.

head: Time after impact
What happens
rows: Impact. The body starts to decelerate sharply, the sensors register the acceleration
The SRS unit has accumulated enough change in speed and deceleration above the threshold — the decision is made
Current flows to the igniter, the pyro charge ignites the inflator tablets, the cover opens along the seam
The airbag is inflated; the driver’s chest and head are just reaching it
The driver enters the airbag: gas escapes through the vent holes, the belt absorbs energy with force limiting
The airbag deflates, the driver returns to the seat back

blocks.x: Why distance from the steering wheel matters

The airbag has to finish inflating before the driver’s chest reaches the cover. If you sit too close, it opens straight into the chest, and the load, instead of a soft deceleration, becomes a blow. That is why manufacturers recommend leaving at least 25 cm between the chest and the airbag cover, and tilting the steering wheel toward the chest rather than the face.
Parts and repair: what to replace after deployment
Airbags are single-use parts. If a Copart or IAAI lot says the airbags deployed, it is not a death sentence but a separate line in the estimate. Here is what a repair usually includes.

head: Part
Replace?
Comment
rows: Single-use. Every deployed module must be replaced, not “recharged”
They fire together with the airbag, usually the whole belt assembly is replaced
Stores the crash record; at many manufacturers it must be replaced or programmed at a dealer
The passenger airbag opens through the dashboard and tears it
Checked for deformation and damage to the module mounting
The ribbon can tear during impact or deployment, the SRS light stays on constantly
Replaced if they are in the deformation zone; without them the system does not work
A sensor error disables the passenger airbag
The passenger airbag strikes the glass, leaving cracks

blocks.x: The cost depends on the make, the number of deployed modules and whether the dashboard has to be replaced. That is why repair is calculated as a separate line for each specific lot — just like on the lot page, which has a repair estimate and a note on the condition of the airbags. There are no universal figures “for all cars”. The general approach to estimating is in the [[guide to repair after auction|repair-guide]].

x: **Do not fit “dummies” and emulators.** A resistor instead of a module turns off the SRS light, but there is no airbag. Check the car with a scanner, not by the light on the dashboard.
**Do not buy counterfeit modules.** US regulators warn about fake airbags that may fail to deploy or fly apart in fragments. Buy only new parts from the manufacturer or a trusted supplier.
**Do not fit a used airbag from an unknown car.** An airbag is a safety part: it has an age, storage conditions and a history.
**Check recall campaigns.** Inflators from several manufacturers have been subject to mass recalls; [[check the VIN|vin-check]] against the manufacturer’s recall database.

faq.q: Does the airbag deploy in every crash?
faq.a: No. Frontal airbags are designed for a head-on impact of roughly 15–25 km/h into a rigid barrier or harder; in a rear-end collision, a light contact or a careful bump against a curb they are not needed. For side impacts and rollovers, side airbags and curtains with their own sensors do the work.

faq.q: Why does the airbag deploy so fast?
faq.a: There is very little time: there are 25–30 cm between the chest and the wheel, and braking takes fractions of a second. The airbag has to fill in 30–40 ms, while the driver has not yet reached the wheel. That is why burning a solid propellant is used rather than a cylinder of compressed gas.

It is a very fast but controlled burn: the charge in the inflator burns in tens of milliseconds, the hot gas is cooled in the filter and enters the airbag. A loud bang and smoke are normal companions of deployment.

faq.q: Can you drive the car after deployment?
faq.a: Not without replacing the modules and belts and checking the SRS unit: the protection does not work after a crash. If you are choosing a lot marked “Airbags: Deployed”, treat the replacement as a separate line in the estimate and plan for a scanner check after the repair.
